text_blocks.snippet: Several medications can lower blood sugar levels, primarily used for managing diabetes. These include insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, and others.
snippet_highlighted_words: insulin, sulfonylureas, thiazolidinediones, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists

text_blocks.snippet: 1. Insulin: This is a hormone naturally produced by the pancreas that helps glucose (sugar) enter cells for energy. People with type 1 diabetes and some with type 2 diabetes require insulin injections to regulate blood sugar.
2. Sulfonylureas: These oral medications stimulate the pancreas to release more insulin. Examples include glimepiride (Amaryl), glipizide (Glucotrol), and glyburide (Micronase, Glynase, Diabeta).

3. Thiazolidinediones (TZDs): These drugs, like rosiglitazone (Avandia) and pioglitazone (Actos), help insulin work more effectively in muscle and fat cells and reduce glucose production in the liver.

4. SGLT2 Inhibitors: These medications, with names ending in "-gliflozin" (e.g., canagliflozin, empagliflozin, dapagliflozin), work by preventing the kidneys from reabsorbing glucose, leading to its elimination in the urine.

5. GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: These injectable medications, such as dulaglutide (Trulicity), exenatide (Byetta, Bydureon), liraglutide (Saxenda, Victoza), and semaglutide (Ozempic, Rybelsus, Wegovy), slow digestion and can also help with weight loss and potentially reduce the risk of heart attack and stroke, according to the Mayo Clinic.

list.title: Metformin:
list.snippet: A common first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes, it reduces glucose production in the liver and improves insulin sensitivity.

list.title: DPP-4 Inhibitors:
list.snippet: These medications, like linagliptin (Tradjenta), saxagliptin (Onglyza), and sitagliptin (Januvia), help increase insulin levels and decrease glucagon levels.

list.title: Glucosidase Inhibitors:
list.snippet: These drugs, like acarbose and miglitol, slow down the breakdown of carbohydrates in the intestines, helping to prevent rapid increases in blood sugar levels.
